packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payments by 23% at six months but did not reduce credit card debt, and it lowered autopay enrollment while increasing missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment (nudge in autopay enrollment default) on real credit-card accounts, six-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a nudge can move an enrollment-like behavioral metric without moving the real financial outcome, and can create new harms — the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk the support team is warning about for round-up sign-ups.
limitations: Credit-card debt paydown context, not a savings product
no measure of amount saved or persistence beyond six months
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests whether a choice-architecture nudge that raises a headline behavioral metric also improves the substantive outcome, the crux of the brief's enrollment-vs-vanity trade-off.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by 0.3%, because employees leave firms, withdraw balances, and opt out of escalation.
packets.methodology: Analysis of administrative data from nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later once withdrawal and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: Retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives income-share effects rather than app-comparable enrolment/engagement rates
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, which the brief asked us to test against.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Across experiments including a 4,207-person five-country European study, default nudges produce medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking, but also lower ratings of the wealth manager's advice — especially when the targeted default is refused — mediated by perceived honesty.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment on default framing in investment advice.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU reputational-risk question in the brief: a default that shapes behavior can simultaneously damage users' trust in the institution, especially when rejected — a caution for how the round-up default and its exit flow should be framed.
limitations: Wealth-management investment context rather than a round-up savings pot
no persistence data beyond the experimental session
packets.relevance_reason: European consumer-finance evidence on when a default reads as manipulative rather than helpful, exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost, and adding a lower preset menu option captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu-design simulations.
packets.why_it_matters: The friction-decomposition method and the counterfactual of adding a lower preset menu tier transfer directly to designing the round-up multiplier menu: it shows how a lower tier can recover most of the welfare loss from anchoring without abandoning presets.
limitations: Tipping decisions at point-of-sale, not a savings product
single-city taxi population, not banking-app users
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: its decomposition of default adherence into deviation-cost and opt-out-cost frictions, and its counterfactual of adding a lower menu option, is a directly applicable technique for designing the round-up multiplier menu.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for downstream (later) effects of default choice architecture, identifying time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist.
packets.methodology: Theoretical review and research-agenda paper synthesizing prior consumer-behavior findings, abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a general, consumer-behavior (not employer-plan) framework for predicting when a default's initial enrollment effect will or will not persist and who it will affect differently — useful for designing the 6-12 month measurement plan.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical, no new effect sizes
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: A recent, consumer-focused theoretical synthesis of exactly the persistence and heterogeneity questions the brief asks about.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, framing pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture practices as regulable when they undermine informed consumer decision-making.
packets.methodology: Doctrinal/normative legal analysis of EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly bears on the entry-design decision: it tells us where the line sits between a helpful opt-out default and a regulable dark pattern under EU law, which is the reputational and legal risk the brief flags for opt-out enrolment.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical behavioural evidence
no financial-product-specific case studies or effect sizes
EU law framework, not a test of any particular default design
packets.relevance_reason: Gives the EU-specific manipulation/dark-pattern framework the brief explicitly asks for when weighing opt-out against active choice.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: With a very high 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees still had not opted out after 12 months (vs. ~50% opt-out under lower defaults elsewhere), and many stayed anchored at 12% even though it was a suboptimal, unmatched contribution rate, especially lower-income employees.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from one employer's retirement plan with a 12% default; compared against a literature review of lower-default opt-out rates.
packets.why_it_matters: Strong quantitative evidence that a pre-set default anchors people at a level many would not have chosen and that this anchoring effect is stronger for lower-income (less sophisticated) users — directly relevant to how we choose the pre-selected multiplier and to the brief's who's-helped/who's-hurt question.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed app
no EU regulatory context
single-employer, 12-month horizon only
packets.relevance_reason: Quantifies default anchoring and shows distributional harm to less-sophisticated savers, both core sub-questions of the brief.
packets.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
packets.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). The findings and conclusions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent the views of SSA, any agency of the Federal Government, the RRC, the authors’ universities, or NBER. The authors thank Joshua Rauh and two anonymous reviewers for their comments and thank Yeguang Chi and Richard Lombardo for excellent research assistance. The authors also acknowledge individual and collective financial support from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-AG021650 and T32-AG-000186) and the Pershing Square Fund for Research on the Foundations of Human Behavior.

packets.key_finding: At three large firms, automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate and fund, and half remained at the default rate/fund after three years.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
packets.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level strongly anchors the level people end up at for years, directly bearing on whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users below a higher tier.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
predates the fintech/liquidity/regulatory context the brief says has changed
packets.relevance_reason: The classic evidence for level-anchoring on pre-set defaults, the exact mechanism the brief worries about for the round-up multiplier choice.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrollment when a straight default is infeasible or ethically fraught, explicitly proposed as a complement to automatic enrollment in savings contexts.
packets.methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature plus a series of studies including two field experiments; abstract-only for effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: This is the direct evidence base for the third onboarding option the brief is weighing — whether active choice captures most of the enrolment benefit without the opt-out disengagement cost — and it offers a concrete design variant (loss-framed active choice) the team could implement instead of a plain forced choice.
limitations: primary experiments are in medication-adherence, not financial, settings
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes for the savings analogy
does not report persistence/withdrawal outcomes
packets.relevance_reason: Directly addresses active choice vs. defaults and proposes a specific enhanced-active-choice mechanism the brief's onboarding decision could adopt.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but ~80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half were still at the default rate and fund after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gain in aggregate wealth accumulation.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment.
packets.why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that defaults raise nominal enrolment but strongly anchor the contribution level and persist for years — exactly the anchoring-versus-vanity-enrolment tension the brief wants tested, giving the benchmark persistence figures (half still at default after 3 years).
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, pre-dates modern fintech/app context
no EU regulatory framing
locked, illiquid savings vehicle unlike round-up sums
packets.relevance_reason: The foundational study on default persistence and anchoring that the newer, more relevant papers in this set are responding to.
packets.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41M observations, ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to active-choice subsidies but strongly moved by automatic (default) contributions, while the 15% of 'active savers' who respond to subsidies mostly just shift assets across accounts with $1 of subsidy raising total saving by only ~1 cent.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data (Danish population registers), natural policy variation in subsidies vs. automatic employer contributions.
alternates.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence on who is actually helped by defaults vs. active-choice mechanisms, and on the size of the gap — sets the effect-size ceiling and the distributional lens the brief asks us to apply, even though the setting is retirement rather than liquid savings.
limitations: employer/government-mediated retirement accounts, not a self-directed consumer app
Danish institutional context, not EU fintech regulatory setting
does not address active-choice-at-onboarding designs directly
alternates.relevance_reason: Foundational large-N evidence on default vs. active-choice effectiveness and on heterogeneous 'active' vs 'passive' saver types, informing the distributional criterion.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months across over 100 US plans and a UK panel, are substantially attenuated by 36 months, though inequality reduction persists; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Observational analysis of administrative data from 100+ US retirement plans and a UK panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete effect-size trajectory (12 vs 36 months) for exactly the persistence question the brief asks, and shows distributional (inequality-reducing) benefits can persist even as average gains shrink.
limitations: Employer/government-mandated retirement plans, not a consumer app
small, liquid round-up sums differ substantially from retirement accounts
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly quantifies attenuation of default effects between 12 and 36 months, the exact persistence question the brief poses, despite the employer-mediated setting.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: Random assignment to Medicare Part D default plans shows large, persistent enrollment and drug-utilization effects, with beneficiary passivity remaining nearly insensitive even when the default causes substantial welfare losses.
alternates.methodology: Natural experiments and random assignment to default options among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
alternates.why_it_matters: Provides rigorous causal evidence that default effects can persist strongly even against beneficiaries' own interests, sharpening the brief's distributional question about who is helped versus harmed by defaulting people in.
limitations: Health insurance/drug plan choice, not a liquid consumer savings product
low-income Medicare population differs from app users choosing round-up savings
alternates.relevance_reason: Rigorous, high-profile evidence on persistence and distributional harm of default enrollment in a non-financial-services domain, useful by analogy for the brief's welfare question.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

alternates.key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrolled individuals subsequently actively opt out, with default effects stronger when incentives are high or enrollment status is unknown.
alternates.methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around Germany's public pension auto-enrollment rollout.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows a large headline default effect on participation can coexist with substantial subsequent opt-out, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment produces durable or nominal sign-ups.
limitations: Public pension system with government as intermediary, not a self-directed consumer app
no data on savings amounts or engagement beyond opt-out status
alternates.relevance_reason: Recent, large-scale evidence quantifying both the size of a default effect and the rate of subsequent active opt-out, informing the persistence question.
alternates.title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
alternates.abstract: Default settings strongly increase pension enrollment, especially when savings incentives are high and choices are complex. We show that the effect is weaker when incentives are low, options are simple, and opting out is easy. We study the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pay-as-you-go pension system. We find that automatic enrollment raises participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out. Linking administrative and survey data shows that the default effect is stronger when enrollment incentives are higher and among individuals who lack knowledge of their enrollment status.

alternates.key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance behavioural regularities and reviews interventions — education, defaults, product design, choice architecture — that firms and governments use to shape financial decisions, without a single new effect-size estimate.
alternates.methodology: Narrative review chapter (abstract-only, no systematic-review protocol stated).
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the broad landscape of choice-architecture interventions in consumer (not just employer-plan) financial behaviour, useful context for weighing product-design levers like preset multipliers against blank fields, but not a source of a decision-specific number.
limitations: review chapter, not a primary study with effect sizes for our decisions
covers many domains beyond savings defaults
not EU-specific or app-specific
alternates.relevance_reason: Broad review of choice architecture in consumer finance that satisfies the brief's request for a synthesis piece, though it lacks decision-specific numbers.
alternates.title: Behavioral Household Finance
alternates.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.
